content.title: About
content.content: Pastrami is a smoked and cured meat, most commonly made from beef brisket, that is seasoned with a blend of spices, dried, and hot‑smoked. Traditional pastrami may also be prepared from turkey or pork. It has a distinctive smoky aroma, a peppery‑sweet flavor, and a tender yet slightly firm texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pastrami originated in Romania as „pastramă“ and was brought to the United States by Jewish immigrants.
The classic spice mix includes coriander, black pepper, paprika, garlic, and mustard seed.
In New York City, pastrami is famously served on rye bread with mustard and pickles.
Thinly sliced cold pastrami is a staple of deli “pastrami‑on‑rye” sandwiches.
Smoking is usually done at 120‑130 °C (250‑265 °F) for several hours.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pastrami provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: The red meat supplies heme iron, which aids oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pastrami contains B12, B6, and niacin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: With virtually no carbs, pastrami fits well into low‑carb dietary patterns.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc in pastrami supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Because it is cured, pastrami is salty and should be limited by people with hypertension.

items.title: Nitrites and nitrates
items.content: Curing and smoking can introduce nitrites, which in large amounts are considered potentially harmful.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beef or other meats used in pastrami.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Pastrami contains roughly 250 kcal per 100 g, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pastrami is typically served thinly sliced cold: in sandwiches, salads, as a snack, or as part of appetizer platters. It can also be gently reheated in a skillet or oven to enhance its smoky flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pastrami in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C (32‑39 °F) for up to 5‑7 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a vacuum‑sealed bag for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or a slimy surface; discard if any signs of spoilage appear.

content.title: About
content.content: Raspberries are the edible berries of the Rubus idaeus shrub. Fresh raspberries are bright red, sweet‑tart, and have a delicate, slightly fragile texture. They are harvested in season (June‑August) and enjoyed fresh or used in cooking, baking, desserts, juices, and jams.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Raspberries belong to the rose family and are closely related to blackberries and blueberries.
Each berry is composed of many small drupelets, each containing a seed.
Fresh raspberries provide over 30 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, making them an excellent source of this vitamin.
They are rich in antioxidants, especially anthocyanins, which give the fruit its vivid color.
In ancient Roman medicine, raspberries were used as a remedy for colds and digestive complaints.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, helps maintain satiety, and assists in blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and quercetin protect cells from oxidative stress and may lower the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Flavonoids in raspberries improve vessel function and can help reduce blood pressure.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 g of fresh raspberries contain about 52 kcal, making them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to raspberries, ranging from skin rash to swelling or breathing difficulties.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Raspberries are often treated with pesticides; thorough washing before consumption is recommended.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raspberries can be eaten fresh, added to yogurt, oatmeal, smoothies, salads, baked goods, and desserts. They can be made into jam, sauces, or cordial. For a longer shelf life, lightly dry them in the oven to create dried fruit.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh raspberries in the refrigerator in an airtight container, preferably on the middle shelf where temperature is stable. Consume within 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze the berries in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag.
